summary.text: A 76-year-old man with a history of chemoradiotherapy for esophageal cancer, type 2 diabetes mellitus and mitral regurgitation had a long intestinal decompression tube placed for intestinal obstruction caused by cecal cancer, then underwent open ileocecal resection on hospital day 8.

An SSI on POD 3 required suture removal and wound irrigation; on POD 6 fascial dehiscence with bowel evisceration required emergency reoperation for fascial repair, leaving the superficial layer open.

NPWT at 125 mmHg started immediately, was switched to NPWTi-d on rPOD 2 for mild wound-bed contamination, and Sorbact was applied on rPOD 9 for extensive necrotic tissue with NPWTi-d continued. The wound bed was cleared by rPOD 21 (standard NPWT), NPWT stopped on rPOD 33 for favorable granulation, and the wound was closed with primary epidermal sutures under general anesthesia on rPOD 34.

summary.text: A 94-year-old man with angina treated with coronary artery bypass grafting and second-degree atrioventricular block treated with pacemaker implantation presented with abdominal pain and was diagnosed with sigmoid colon perforation and acute generalized peritonitis, requiring an emergency Hartmann procedure.

Wound redness on POD 9 led to partial suture removal and irrigation; on POD 10 worsened redness and purulent discharge led to removal of all sutures and NPWTi-d at 125 mmHg, with debridement as needed and wound management planned three times weekly. On POD 19 severe infection with partial communication with the abdominal cavity (abstract: partial fascial dehiscence with bowel exposure) and extensive necrotic tissue were treated by adding Sorbact while continuing NPWTi-d at 125 mmHg.

Irrigation was stopped and topical NPWT used from POD 30; NPWT ended by POD 38 with markedly improved granulation. The patient was transferred on POD 40, so complete epithelialization and the time of final healing were not confirmed.

summary.text: A 77-year-old man with emphysema presented with abdominal pain and was found to have rectal cancer perforation with acute generalized peritonitis, requiring an emergency Hartmann procedure.

Wound redness on POD 9 with an SSI was managed by irrigation. On POD 13 worsening redness and swelling and complete suture removal revealed exposed bowel (partial fascial dehiscence, necrotic tissue at the wound base); Sorbact was applied and NPWTi-d started at 125 mmHg. On POD 16 dehiscence worsened with increased bowel exposure and negative pressure was reduced to 50 mmHg with NPWTi-d continued.

On POD 24 necrosis had decreased with dermal-like tissue growth and epithelialization over the exposed bowel, prompting a switch to NPWT; pressure was adjusted to 75 mmHg on POD 26. NPWT was completed and the upper wound closed with sutures on POD 40. On POD 55 the wound was fully epithelialized and the patient was transferred for rehabilitation.

article_limitations: Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; actual 4 JPEGs inspected in the separate visual submission.

Protocol statements in b00010 (normal saline instillation, dressing changes every 48-72 h, starting pressure 125 vs 50 mmHg, definition of wound healing) are stated for the institutional protocol, not individually for each patient, and were not copied to individual patients as facts; patient-specific pressures come from each case narrative.

Discussion durations (healing within 28-32 days after NPWTi-d initiation in 2 cases; 29 days in one case) are aggregate and are not assigned to patients; case 2 final healing is explicitly unconfirmed.
Case 3 POD 55 wound state differs between text (fully epithelialized) and Fig. 4 caption (sutured closed).
Cause of case 2 sigmoid perforation, histology/stage of cecal and rectal cancers, and diagnostic tests are not described.
No laboratory, imaging or microbiology results are reported for any patient; observations are not documented.

Series-level statement "In our series, no bowel perforation or related complications were observed" (b00018) is not copied to individual patients (rule NO-COHORT-COPY); likewise the aggregate healing durations in b00019.
